stories.headline: Why Fever coach Stephanie White has the toughest job in sports
stories.summary: She has the stars but also the strife. Stephanie White is fortifying her locker room as storms swirl around Indiana's championship hopes.
stories.body:
STEPHANIE WHITE KNOWS how good she has it coaching the Indiana Fever. In 25 seconds in June, Caitlin Clark shook her defender for a step-back 3, Aliyah Boston blocked a driving Angel Reese, and Kelsey Mitchell beat everyone up the court for an easy layup. A big three featuring two of the best young superstars in the WNBA in Clark and Boston and a veteran scoring machine in Mitchell. From a basketball perspective, it's hard to beat that balance of win-now with sustainability.

The Fever play in packed arenas at home and on the road. Fans fill Gainbridge Fieldhouse, to the tune of 16,426 per game. Fever No. 22 jerseys invade rival arenas. A Fever national TV game can attract more than a million viewers, something no regular-season game could sniff in the pre-Clark era.

"When the ball goes up in a game, I love it," White says. "I love the chess match. I love the intensity. I love the competition. I love putting players in positions to try to be successful."

She also knows how tough she has it.

Across 74 days of this 2026 WNBA season, White clashed with Clark, and the sharpest shouters on social media called for her head. She was bombarded by demonstrators who wanted to leverage the Fever to make political statements about transgender athletes. She was booed at home.

Social media lights up with criticism of White's perceived mistakes, dissecting her interactions with players and her postgame comments to reporters. Players are animated on the court and vocal in the world. Fans are impatient for a championship, and trolls are quick to point out flaws.

"There's an infatuation with our team, and there's an infatuation with some of our players, and there's a lot of negativity that surrounds anything that's different from what the fandom wants to see," White says. "And that is challenging as a coach to navigate."

Starting Sunday, White and the Fever embark on the playoffs, where the spotlight burns brightest and voices grow loudest. To win, White will need more than Clark 3-pointers and Boston rebounds. She'll need support in the stands and unity in the locker room. Harmony produces victory, and White needs nine more for the Fever to reach their goal. It might be the most difficult calculus in sports.

"I think the vortex of everything that we deal with, with our team and our franchise, is definitely challenging," White says. "It's hard to escape it."

WHITE IS THOUSANDS of miles away when Briann January sits in the glitziest room the Indiana Fever have to offer. The assistant coach and former Fever player squeezes her right hand into a fist. She opens her hand back up. She subconsciously closes it and shapes another fist.

January has spent 10 of her 39 years playing for or working with Stephanie White, and she has been riding sidecar with the Fever head coach throughout this whiplash-inducing season.

Sitting across from me while White helps coach the national team in Germany, January shakes her head. And closes her fist.

Relaxing against the plush gray fabric of her chair, surrounded by a golden hue of the bar behind her, she tells me her repeated hand movement isn't a nervous tic or a practice playcall. "That's a Steph thing," she says.

She tells me she is channeling White on this muggy September day. Across 3,000 miles of ocean and 625 miles of land and four regular-season games to go. The Fever are 26-14 and have the talent to win a title. But the criticism is never-ending and resolve has its limits.

Close the fist. It's a symbol for when it's time to fight.

Close this fist. It's a symbol for team unity.

Close the fist. It's a call to action.

"If you go to hit somebody with an open hand, you might make a red mark," January says. "But if you're swinging with the fists, with a closed fist together, you can do some damage. And that's ... we have to stay strong, and we're strongest when we are together, when we're connected, and that's the whole thing."

THE FEVER'S CONNECTION showed signs of crumbling early on. During a May 30 game in Portland, White laid into Clark on the bench. The star fired back, gesturing in frustration. White motioned for backup point guard Raven Johnson to take Clark's place on the bench. Clark stood up and drank from her water bottle while the timeout finished. Johnson entered the game and Indiana lost 100-84 and dropped to 4-4 to start the season.

A video of the interaction circulated on social media, driving calls for the Fever to choose between White and Clark. It was a far cry from how the previous season ended, when White was lauded for steering the Fever to Game 5 of the semifinals against the Las Vegas Aces despite missing multiple injured players, including Clark and Sophie Cunningham.

"We were an underdog," former Fever general manager Lin Dunn says of last season's playoff push. "We were just scrambling, trying to figure out a way to do this. Bandage that one, pull this one, pick up another one. Expectations were not as high. With Caitlin back and healthy, everybody healthy, expectations go up. So you have to adapt and adjust to what they are."

The Fever largely did at the start of the 2026 season. On June 11, Clark and Boston became the first teammates in league history to have a 30-point double-double in the same game. Later that month, Cunningham, a reserve guard and steadfast enforcer, drew a slew of new admirers -- and some detractors -- for defending Clark and pointing her finger at DeWanna Bonner. On July 17, Clark scored a career-high 45 points and 10 assists to record the first 40-10 game in WNBA history. All the while, Mitchell poured in points at a historic pace. Boston, Mitchell and Clark were all named All-Star starters and Indiana took a 17-10 record into the break. White was named the WNBA's Coach of the Month in July.

The serenity would soon be snapped.

In a July 21 article on ESPN.com, Cunningham shared that she supported barring transgender girls and women from girls' and women's sports.

"I got a lot of negative feedback about me hating trans. And I'm like, 'I never once said that,'" she said. "I think that I am here to extend love. But I also think with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men."

Demonstrations supporting Cunningham and counterdemonstrations followed Indiana around the country for the rest of July into August. Players and coaches were asked their opinions on transgender athletes, a hotly debated topic.

"I don't know that I would say that I'm educated enough from a scientific standpoint," White said ahead of the Fever's game in Portland on July 31. "I don't ever believe that exclusion is an answer. I just don't. I do think, when we think about various levels of sport, various governing bodies of sport and things that go into that. As I said, I'm not educated enough at the different levels. I know growing up that I played with the boys all the time."

The controversy exploded when former NBA players Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White declared they were eligible for the WNBA draft on Aug. 7. Advocates for excluding transgender and intersex women pressured the WNBA to clarify its policy, but the league resisted.

"There are no immediate eligibility matters affecting the WNBA and we strongly denounce the bad-faith efforts to use these topics to demean or marginalize others," the WNBA said in an Aug. 12 statement.

Then, on Aug. 23, Kanter Freedom sat courtside when Indiana visited Chicago. He was ejected, and later banned from the arena, following a confrontation with Sky guard Natasha Cloud. Royce White showed up to the Fever's Aug. 28 game against the Sun wearing a blond wig.

Through it all, the Fever kept playing -- and scoring. The team boasts the league's top offensive rating at 117.0. They surpassed 100 points a league-record 20 times this season.

"I think that people have these expectations of our group and our team as if we are like superhumans, man," Mitchell says. "Like we got superpowers and s---. And as a coach, they probably think that she has superpowers."

Omniscience isn't one of them.

"This has not been anything that I've experienced before at this level, right?" White says. "So, for me, it's trying to learn how I can weather the storm."

Make that storms. Another one already was brewing. And tracking even closer to home.

WHITE DEFINES HERSELF as a purist. She's a real-life Jimmy Chitwood from an even smaller Indiana town than fictional Hickory or Milan, the town "Hoosiers" was based on. As of the 2020 census, a little under 700 people live in White's hometown of West Lebanon, Indiana, a town snuggled next to the Illinois border in Warren County.

White often says a lot of words when she gets on a roll, but she doesn't speak quickly. She thinks through each sentence, often pausing with an "um," that sits at the back of her mouth. She loves to use a refrain -- like a pastor -- to hammer home a point. She has a thick Indiana accent, adding a sing-song lilt on her r's and l's. It almost sounds Southern, but it's from the Indiana countryside. The kind of accent found in the rural counties where cornfields and cows outnumber people.

Born to young parents with very little money, basketball was a refuge.

"Basketball was my lifeline," White says. "Like it was my savior."

She met Dunn in elementary school and was a regular at her camps. She practically lived in the gym. She would go shoot when she was pissed off or needed a break.

After high school, she journeyed some 35 miles beyond the West Lebanon town line to West Lafayette to play for Dunn at Purdue. In 1999, White was named the winner of the Wade Trophy and led Purdue to its first -- and still only -- national championship. After averaging 17.2 points, 5.3 rebounds and 4.6 assists over her four seasons with the Boilermakers, she was drafted in the second round by the Charlotte Sting, where she played for one season. She was traded in 2000 to the expansion Fever, who averaged 11,266 fans per game in their inaugural season. She played four seasons with the Fever and retired after the 2004 season, when the Fever's average attendance was 7,589.

Basketball, remember, is her life. After spending time on college staffs as an assistant, White took a job as an assistant coach with the Chicago Sky. Dunn and Fever president Kelly Krauskopf intervened in 2011 and brought White to Indiana. Even as a young assistant, she craved having a ball in her hands and worked out her frustrations by pounding it on the hardwood or chasing the high of a swish. When Dunn retired, White took the head job in 2015 and led Indiana all the way to the finals after starting the season 1-4. Following the 2016 season, White left for Vanderbilt. She was fired in 2021 after the Commodores opted out of the season due to injuries, illness and scheduling difficulties due to COVID-19.

"Sport and life is a series of failures, right?" White says. "It's what you do with those failures."

In 2023, seven years after she'd last coached in the pros, White returned to the WNBA to coach the Connecticut Sun. Former MVP Jonquel Jones had been traded to the Liberty. Still, White led the Sun to the semifinals in her first season. She did it again in her second.

"This game is evolving, all the time, and she's a consistent learner," January says. "She never thinks she knows it all, and I think that's why she's been successful."

Dunn had returned to the Fever in 2022. Krauskopf returned from working across the street with the Pacers in 2024. With Dunn and Krauskopf back with the Fever, White came home ahead of the 2025 season.

She had observed the Fever spotlight from afar in Connecticut. At the onset of Clark-mania, the Fever averaged more than 17,000 fans in 2024 and regularly drew a million viewers for televised games. White had seen for herself the venomous and racialized response to the Sun's DiJonai Carrington poking Clark in the eye in a postseason game in 2024.

White harbored some trepidation about what coaching in Indiana would be like in this new reality. The fame. The fans. The impact on her partner and sons.

"There's a difference in being critical and in being a jerk," White says. "So that's more in reference to protecting my family and protecting my peace."

Did she ever stand a chance?

A DAY AFTER Kanter Freedom announced his draft eligibility, Cunningham saw nothing but blue Sky paint ahead on her way to a breakaway layup in Chicago. But Carrington chased her down and swatted her left arm across Cunningham's face and neck. Cunningham fell hard to the floor before confronting Carrington.

The referees assessed a flagrant 2 foul on the play and ejected Carrington, who had played two seasons under White at Connecticut.

"One of the things about Nai is that she's going to play her butt off, man," White said after the game. "She's going to compete. Nobody is going to go walking in for a layup. I don't oppose the hard foul but I also don't think she intentionally went for the neck."

The perceived pro-Carrington comment infuriated Fever fans. Indiana's Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith posted on X calling for White's firing. "The Indiana Fever need to let Stephanie White go. No solid coach would ever take the side of the opposing team's player who committed a flagrant foul on one of your own players. Terrible coaching! The Fever need to defend their players."

White long ago deleted social media from her phone, intentionally creating a barrier between fans and critics and her ear. But this storm was powerful and her barriers were not impenetrable.

"I don't typically get caught up in it, but I was hurt with the implications of me not caring about my players," White says.

She decided she needed to say something on the drive to Gainbridge on Aug. 11. It had been three days of unending criticism and indictments of her character.

White later said that she had not seen the clip in full. But she prides herself on her relationships with players, past and present. As well as her integrity. "I just felt compelled because you don't know me," White says. "And you don't get to say that."

White spoke with Cunningham after she saw the full clip and the intensity of the foul. White told her that she'd never intentionally have another player's back, former or not, over her own team.

"That was between me and DiJonai, and people try to make things weird between me and Steph," Cunningham tells me. "I know that if I ever needed anything, that she's going to show up 100% and give me love and give me whatever I need."

Before the Fever took on the Liberty that Aug. 11 night, White, wearing a red leather jacket and speaking through her own emotion, gave a fiery statement condemning the rhetoric around her team and the league.

"This is more for an online community trying to create narratives that simply don't exist, trying to create a fabrication or distortion of who I am and what I'm about," she said. "Our players' success, our players' health and wellness, and our players' safety is always a top priority for me."

She ended by saying, "Love will win. Grace will win. Humility will win. And kindness will win. I stand by them, I will always stand by them. Everybody else can go to hell."

She grabbed the paper with the statement and stormed off the dais.

She gets emotional talking about it with me now.

"You don't get to create a narrative about who I am," White says. "I was not going to personally be hijacked like our league is being hijacked."

An hour after her speech, the raucous cheers for the Fever players dissipated when White's name echoed through the speakers. The cheers were replaced by a chorus of boos.

White's players heard it.

"It was just weird for all of us to be honest," Cunningham says. "Because at the end of the day, you got to show respect. That's our head coach, and we're proud to play for her."

White's staff heard it.

"It pissed me off, if I'm gonna be completely honest," January says. "it just doesn't make sense to me, you know. And it's just very disrespectful."

Clark walked over to White and embraced her. She told her coach that she loved her, that the team had this one. The Fever defeated the Liberty 106-92. After the game, sitting at the dais for her postgame news conference, Clark didn't mince words.

"I hated that our fans booed her before the game," Clark said. "It made me a little sick to be honest."

White heard the boos too. How could she not? She felt them too.

She once believed that the noise around the Fever, the criticism, the obsession, the politics, that it all existed outside of Gainbridge. It was online. It was on television, but White could change the channel. Sometimes it was in news conferences, but the media left eventually. But that day, the noise infiltrated her home, her sanctuary, and it was directed at her.

"It hurt," White says to me now. "But at the same time, I think it was a moment of realization that this is not what it used to be.

"I mean it. Everybody else can go to hell."

HER 49-YEAR-OLD body no longer allows her to take refuge in the gym like she once did. Now White journals and meditates. Her pen has been getting a workout this season.

She also occasionally makes time for "Ted Lasso." She dressed as the titular character for Halloween one year. It's easy to see why she loves the show and Ted. White and Lasso share an earnestness and naivety (complimentary). White strives every day to get the most out of her players and work toward another championship for the Fever. Her drive isn't much more complicated than that. It's everything else that comes with the job that creates the complication.

And the one thing that sticks in her craw more than anything else are the assumptions.

There's a scene in the first season of "Ted Lasso" where Lasso was challenged to a game of darts. His challenger assumed that Lasso would be bad. But Lasso had grown up playing darts with his late father. Lasso won the match and the bet.

"Often when you don't know people, you assume things," White says. "Everyone is dealing with life experiences that we know nothing about. Sometimes we'll find out. Sometimes we won't."

White gets asked a lot if she still finds joy in the game. There's plenty to not love about what's happening around the WNBA right now, she says.

"The racism, the homophobia, the sexism, like all that stuff," White says. "That's just ridiculous. I often say it's not that hard to not be a jerk, but maybe it is. ... Maybe it's hard to be nice."

Against the Lynx on Sept. 22, White was trying to do just that. Clark cut to the basket late in the second quarter at Gainbridge Fieldhouse and caught a pass from Boston in stride. Nia Brodie fouled Clark as she went up for the reverse, and Clark landed on her butt, legs outstretched facing the Fever bench. White rushed from the sideline holding out her arms and helped her superstar guard off the hardwood. The Fever were up by 27. The moment looked pleasant and encouraging and innocuous. But not to everyone. As the clip circulated on X, White was accused of being "performative" and trying to save her job.

"I love my players," White says. "They know that. Every player that I've ever had knows that."

So-called lip readers and body-language experts have been doing this all season to White, to January too. Really to anyone within a country mile of Clark.

January tells me she's had a taste of what White goes through. Clips of January coaching Clark have popped up on social media too, roiling fans who think January has it out for the star Fever guard.

"I'm very passionate about this game. I'm passionate about this team," says January, who spent nine of her 14 WNBA seasons playing for Indiana. "At the end of the day, we know [Clark] can be great, and we're not going to let her off the hook. After those things, C and I are good. If we're good, I don't understand why everybody's not good. But that's something they can carry, and we're going to continue on to try and be the best team we can."

It's the part of the job White loves most. And she still gets that warmth of joy when the ref tosses the ball in the air and sneakers squeak against the hardwood and whistles pierce through the cacophony of the arena.

"When it's about basketball, and you're in there, and you're with these women, and you know they're working their butts off, it's what I love," White says. "When I stop loving that, I think that's the moment to be done."

WHITE ISN'T SURE when she started saying "close the fist," but she's been saying it for a long time.

The fist is about team over individual. "Each of the fingers is part of our ego," she says. "None of us get to where we are without one."

It's about intention. "You can't close your fingers without intentionally doing it," she says of closing a fist. "What happens when you're not focused on it? It's open."

Her smirk is practically audible through the phone.

"Five fingers can do a lot of things," she says. "But a fist packs a punch."

Like January, she makes a fist as she's talking about it. At least that's what she says.

This Indiana Fever season has been absurd and amazing. It's been joyous and heartbreaking. White still feels the sting. From the fouls and the fans and the fame.

And from the finish. The Fever scored their fewest points of the season in an 86-66 loss to the top-seeded Lynx on Thursday night in their final regular-season game. Boston and reserve guard Ty Harris left the game with injuries. Clark went 1-for-12 from the field and 0-for-7 on 3s. She finished with a career-low two points.

"We flush this one," White told reporters after the game. "We learn from it. We grow from it."

Because now it's playoff time. The sixth-seeded Fever open their bid for the franchise's first title since 2012 on Sunday against the defending champion Aces. White knows the time is now for coaches and players to silence the distractions and to take matters into their own hands.

"You don't win without connection," she says. "You don't win without the fist."

stories.headline: Oscar winner Lupita Nyong'o invests in BAL team Nairobi City Thunder
stories.summary: Oscar-winning actress Lupita Nyong'o announced her investment in the Nairobi City Thunder, the first Kenyan team to play at the NBA-backed Basketball Africa League (BAL), on Thursday.
stories.body:
Oscar-winning actress Lupita Nyong'o announced her investment in the Nairobi City Thunder, the first Kenyan team to play at the NBA-backed Basketball Africa League (BAL), on Thursday.

Nyong'o is a citizen of Kenya, Mexico and the United States. She is the daughter of Kenyan politician and academic Peter Anyang' Nyong'o - the incumbent governor of Kisumu County - and Dorothy Nyong'o, a PR consultant who is the managing trustee of the Africa Cancer Foundation.

After her Oscar-winning breakthrough in Steve McQueen's 12 Years a Slave (2013), Mexico City-born Lupita Nyong'o shot to fame and has never looked back.

The actress, who notably starred in Black Panther (2018), Us (2019) and The Odyssey (2026), wrote on Instagram on Thursday: "Taking a tunnel walk to celebrate that I'm an investor in the Nairobi City Thunder!

"The Nairobi City Thunder are the first Kenyan team to qualify for the Basketball Africa League, and I'm pumped and proud to be behind them. TWENDE!

"Big weekend ahead with the start of the KNBL Finals! Wishing everyone on and off the court a great time!!"

The team was founded in 1998 - initially as NSSF Stars and later International Christian Church before switching to its current name in 2010. The 2023 acquisition of the club by Twende Sports Limited -- founded by Colin Rasmussen, Sandra Kimokoti, Kush Diriye and Stephen Domingo -- sparked a new era of success.

In 2025, Nairobi City Thunder became the first Kenyan team to play in the BAL in the fifth season of the league organized by the NBA and FIBA - a feat which they repeated in the tournament's sixth edition this year.

The BAL is transitioning to a franchise model from 2027 onwards, with permanent slots in the league on offer along with limited availability for non-franchise teams seeking to qualify.

Nairobi City Thunder will face Kenya Ports Authority (KPA) in the national finals for a third successive year, having comfortably beaten them in the previous two.

stories.headline: AFL player movement tracker: trade requests, free agency latest, who's on the move?
stories.summary: The offseason is upon us which means AFL trades, free agency, and player movement is about to take off. Here's the latest news, whispers, and confirmed deals.
stories.body:
It's AFL player movement season, with trades and free agency set to dominate the month of October. So who is going where? Keep track with our player movement guide here.

When is the AFL trade and free agency window?
The 2026 AFL trade period commences on Monday, October 5 and closes in the evening of Wednesday, October 14.

The free agency window opens and closes a little ealier; it runs from Friday, October 2 until Friday, October 9.

Friday, Sept. 25
Jordon Butts to join the Bulldogs

Zak Butters isn't the only South Australian-based player keen to join the Western Bulldogs, with Crows' key defender Jordon Butts officially naming the Dogs as his preferred offseason destination.

The unrestricted free agent will sign a five-year deal at the Kennel, according to AFL.com.au.

Tuesday, Sept. 22
Amartey officially names Carlton

Wantaway Sydney forward Joel Amartey has confirmed his desire to join Carlton as an unrestricted free agent.

The 26-year-old was kept out of the Swans' side with an Achilles injury in the latter stages of the year.

With Charlie Curnow (75 goals in 2026) and Logan McDonald (51) cementing their spots in the Sydney forward line as the prime targets, Amartey is hoping for more opportunity at the Blues.

Thursday, Sept. 17
GWS captain finally makes big call on his future

Toby Greene has opted to leave GWS, telling the AFL club he wishes to play with Geelong next season. Greene, who has been at the Giants since their foundation season in 2012, wants to go back to Victoria for family reasons.

In an extraordinary way to announce the decision, outgoing GWS boss Dave Matthews confirmed Greene's intentions on radio, before the club released a statement.

The 32-year-old has been offered a lucrative three-year deal to join the Cats.

Saturday, Sept. 12
Zak Butters makes huge free agency call
The year's hottest restricted free agent Zak Butters has made a huge call on his future, nominating the Western Bulldogs as his preferred destination.

After a year of speculation, with Geelong thought to be the front-runner for the Power star's signature, Butters made the call on Saturday, first reported by AFL.com.au's Callum Twomey.

The deal is reportedly for nine years.

Thursday, Sept. 10
Hogan set to join Pies
GWS and Collingwood have both confirmed that 2024 Coleman Medal winner Jesse Hogan has chosen the Magpies at his next home.

Set to be a four-club player, Hogan is 31 and coming off a 12-goal season from just nine appearances.

It's a big boost for the Magpies if Hogan can recapture his form; key forward has been an area of concern for a number of years.

Tuesday, Sept. 8
Bailey set to be Lion for life
Brisbane's Zac Bailey has ended months of 'will he, won't he' speculation to sign with the Lions for eight years, taking him through the 2034 season, the the club confirmed on Tuesday.

Bailey, a free agent, had been a big target for the Crows, who had reportedly tabled a more lucrative offer.

"I'm absolutely rapt to be staying at the Brisbane Lions," Bailey said in a statement.

"I love the environment here, the players, coaches and staff who all make it a great place to be and I feel like this Club continues to bring the best out of me.

"This Club means so much to me - I came here as a young player and have grown up here and to know I will be here long-term is something I'm really proud of.

"I would like to thank the club, my partner Em, my family and my management for being so supportive throughout this process.

"I love what we as a club have achieved during my time here and I am super excited about what we can continue to achieve together."

Rowan Marshall requests trade
St Kilda ruck Rowan Marshall looks set to be on the move, with the Saints confirming the big man had requested a trade for the second straight season.

While Marshall hasn't requested a specific club, it's likely to be Geelong after he failed to secure a trade to the Cats last year. He played 21 games for the Saints this seaosn, juggling ruck duties with Tom De Koning, who came in from Carlton last offseason.

"Rowan is a highly valued member of the St Kilda Football Club and remains contracted until the end of 2027," the Saints said in a statement.

"Marshall has not nominated a preferred destination at this stage, with the club making clear that any trade will need to be in the best interests of the St Kilda Football Club."

Zane Duursma wants to go to Melbourne
The No. 4 pick in the 2023 AFL draft Zane Duursma has requested a trade out of North Melbourne, with Melbourne in his sights.

The news comes a week after coach Alastair Clarkson was sacked by the club. North won nine games in 2026, their best return since 2019.

Ed Allan re-signs with the Pies
After speculation about his future at the Magpies, mdifielder Ed Allan has put pen to paper, signing a four year extension to remain at Collingwood.

2026 was a breakout season for Allan, who played 19 games and averaged a career-high 16.5 disposals per game.

Monday, Sept. 7
Pair of in-demand Dogs re-sign
According to afl.com.au, both Arty Jones and Buku Khamis will remain at the Kennel this offseason.

Jones will sign a three-year deal, while Khamis has a five-year contract in front of him.

Essendon and Brisbane had interest in livewire forward Jones, who had a standout performance against Collingwood in the wildcard final win, while the Blues were heavily linked to Khamis for a second straight offseason.

Cooper Hodge nomintes Hawthorn
A big boost for the Hawks, with club champion Luke Hodge's son Cooper choosing to join the Melbourne-based team as a father-son at this year's draft.

He had the option of going to Brisbane as a Lions academy member.

Arman Tsarukyan put on a performance at UFC 331 that makes him all but undeniable as the next challenger for the lightweight championship.

Tsarukyan has been in this position before. In January 2025, he pulled out of a title fight because of injury one day before he was to fight for the belt. Later in the year, he was twice passed over when the UFC was booking title bouts. But Saturday's elbow to the face of Mauricio Ruffy gave Tsarukyan the impressive first-round knockout he needed to position himself as the likely first challenger of champion Justin Gaethje.

Tsarukyan's victory also boosted him above former champion Ilia Topuria to No. 2 at lightweight in the latest ESPN divisional rankings.

stories.headline: Borussia Dortmund teenager Konstantinos Karetsas returns to training after Champions League health scare
stories.summary: Borussia Dortmund says 18-year-old midfielder Konstantinos Karetsas is back in training just over a week after he slumped to the ground in an alarming medical incident on his Champions League debut.
stories.body:
Borussia Dortmund have said 18-year-old midfielder Konstantinos Karetsas is back in training just over a week after he slumped to the ground in an alarming medical incident on his Champions League debut.

Karetsas passed the ball to a teammate then signaled his distress to the referee before sitting on the grass during Dortmund's 3-2 win over Villarreal on Sept. 8.

He was in tears as he was stretchered off with suspected circulatory problems and was then taken to a hospital, where he stayed for much of last week.

"Konstantinos Karetsas is back in team training as of Wednesday after doing individual sessions at the start of the week," Dortmund said. "It was his first joint session with his teammates after he was taken off with circulatory problems in the game against Villarreal."

Dortmund hasn't specified the nature of any diagnosis for Karetsas, who was signed from Genk for a reported fee of $34.6 million last month, and didn't indicate whether he would be able to play Saturday against Stuttgart in the Bundesliga.

Karetsas plays internationally for Greece but was born in Belgium, where local media have reported that dehydration was suspected as a factor.

"I'm doing really well," he said in a video recorded during a visit to his old club Genk and published Monday on X. "We tested everything and everything is fine. I just need to adjust a bit to the intensity but that will come with time."

"I went out with him but in that moment, he wasn't able to speak," Book said.

- Borussia Dortmund teenager Karetsas hospitalised after slumping to turf in Champions League

Karetsas was able to cheer on his teammates from the stands in Saturday's 3-0 win over Paderborn.

Managing director Lars Ricken said there had been "no warning signs" of any circulatory problems prior to the incident.

stories.headline: NRL Preliminary Finals: Teams, line-ups, tips, odds, everything you need to know for the weekend
stories.summary: This is it, the weekend when we decide the two teams that will battle it out for the NRL premiership, and we have been presented with two cracking games to determine the grand finalists.
stories.body:
This is it, the weekend when we decide the two teams that will battle it out for the 2026 NRL premiership, and we have been presented with two cracking games to determine the grand finalists. On Friday night we have an attacking masterpiece when the Dolphins host the Roosters, before Sunday sees the giant-killing Knights facing the biggest giant of them all.

Good luck with your tips.

Friday, September 25
Dolphins vs. Sydney Roosters
Suncorp Stadium, 7:50pm (AEST)

Dolphins: 1. Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow 2. Jamayne Isaako 3. Jack Bostock 4. Herbie Farnworth 5. Selwyn Cobbo 6. Kodi Nikorima 7. Isaiya Katoa 8. Thomas Flegler 9. Jeremy Marshall-King 10. Tom Gilbert 11. Max Plath 12. Kulikefu Finefeuiaki 13. Morgan Knowles Bench: 14. Kurt Donoghoe 15. Ray Stone 16. Francis Molo 17. Connelly Lemuelu 18. Felise Kaufusi 19. Brad Schneider Reserves: 20. Jake Averillo

Roosters: 1. James Tedesco 2. Daniel Tupou 3. Billy Smith 4. Robert Toia 5. Mark Nawaqanitawase 6. Daly Cherry-Evans 7. Sam Walker 8. Naufahu Whyte 9. Reece Robson 10. Lindsay Collins 11. Salesi Foketi 12. Siua Wong 13. Victor Radley Bench:14. Connor Watson 15. Angus Crichton 16. Nat Butcher 17. Spencer Leniu 18. Hugo Savala 19. Cody Ramsey Reserves: 22. Benaiah Ioelu

Officials

Referee: Adam Gee Touchies: Phil Henderson, Tyson Brough

Bunker: Ashley Klein

Prediction: The Dolphins were very impressive two weeks ago against the Warriors, restricting them to one try, before unleashing their signature attacking blitz after the break. Previously this season they have allowed teams to get away to big head starts before mounting their fightback, a ploy which just won't stand up in the finals. They appear to have taken note and their defensive work in New Zealand was outstanding. They will need to be at their very best once more against the Roosters, who have the attacking flair to cause them plenty of problems.

The Roosters were simply too good for the Sharks last week, after going very close to beating the Panthers the week before. They have plenty of experience across the park, with Daly Cherry-Evans putting in a much better performance against the Sharks in combination with the hard running Hugo Savala. Outside those two, the Roosters backline bristles with attacking weapons, with Robert Toia and Mark Nawaqanitawase in unstoppable form, James Tedesco always lurking, and Sam Walker returning at halfback.

But, as we all know, the backs don't win the big games, they just determine the score, and the Roosters have a pack that is the match of any in the league. Naufahu Whyte, Lindsay Collins and Siua Wong were at their destructive best against the Sharks. Add the menace of Victor Radley and Spencer Leniu, plus the returning Angus Crichton, and there isn't a weakness across the middle or on the edges.

The Dolphins will have to match the Roosters forwards, with Thomas Flegler, Tom Gilbert, Max Plath, Kulikefu Finefeuiaki, Ray Stone and Francis Molo all in for a big night. If they can negate the Roosters pack, we all know how devastating the Dolphins halves and backs can be.

On paper this is very difficult to pick. It is one of those games that might come down to a key error, a moment of madness, the luck of the bounce or the whims of the referee's six again calls. Whoever wins, we are sure to be treated to an entertaining clash.

Tip: Dolphins by 10

PointsBet odds: Dolphins $1.74 (-2.5 $2) Roosters $2.10 (+2.5 $1.83)

The Panthers didn't have it all their way two weeks ago when defeating the Roosters, they were well-matched and needed a wobbly Nathan Cleary field goal to break a late deadlock. Cleary has been the focus ever since, as first he avoided suspension for a dangerous contact charge, and then set about rehabilitating an injured foot. The Panthers have proven they can win games without Cleary, but his coolness under pressure is invaluable in the biggest games.

The Knights are playing with the casino's money at this stage. After finishing last in 2025, making the finals surpassed anyone's expectations. The Panthers are the best team in the competition for good reason and they stand between the other three teams and the premiership title. I think they'll return to the big dance this year.
